projects.title: Fire, heat & structural damage
projects.subtitle: From an inspectable fire simulation to evidence-based scene and state initialization.
projects.summary: Building an inspectable thermal-damage simulation, then asking how images and building documents can initialize a useful short-term forecast.

sections.title: An inspectable simulation
sections.body: Built an interactive 3D workspace connecting heat diffusion, member temperatures, cumulative damage and failure events, with scenario controls and reproducible run records.

sections.title: Evidence-based initialization
sections.body: The graduation research direction studies how visual observations and building documents can reconstruct a scene and its current fire state for short-term simulation.

sections.title: Current scope
sections.body: A working prototype with simplified, uncalibrated parameters. Multi-source reconstruction and forecast validation remain planned research.

projects.title: VLA models in the driving loop
projects.subtitle: Making driving models testable in a feedback loop.
projects.role: R&D Intern · Dongfeng Motor Corporation R&D Institute
projects.summary: Built VLA inference bridges for Bench2Drive/CARLA and AlpaSim, made evaluation easier to diagnose and repeat, and tested commercial simulation workflows.

sections.title: Integration is part of the experiment
sections.body: I integrated a vision-language-action model with Bench2Drive and CARLA for closed-loop evaluation. This required correcting trajectory coordinates and navigation mappings, and synchronizing camera inputs with ego-vehicle history so the model and simulator described the same state.

sections.title: Tracing inference overhead
sections.body: I identified and removed redundant multi-gigabyte array copies in the ONNX inference path. A route-level benchmark recorded approximately 68 seconds of baseline mean latency and 5.7 seconds of optimized warm-state median latency. These use different summary statistics and operating conditions, so they are reported as observations rather than a universal speedup ratio.

sections.title: Making evaluation recoverable
sections.body: I built a persistent PyTorch inference service and a resumable evaluation pipeline. Isolating simulator and model dependencies helped make the system easier to operate and diagnose, while distinguishing driving failures from simulator and evaluation faults made the resulting evidence more interpretable.

projects.title: Reconstruction beyond one sensor path
projects.subtitle: Baseline evaluation under changes in sensing trajectories.
projects.summary: Comparing physical-field reconstruction baselines when sensors follow trajectories different from the original sensing distribution.

sections.title: The evaluation question
sections.body: A reconstruction method can perform differently when the sensing trajectory changes. My work examines this shift through baseline comparisons, using shared evaluation protocols to make the behavior of different methods comparable.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.body: I evaluated randomized-trajectory fine-tuning and empirical Gaussian-process methods, and compared reconstruction errors across scan and rotated trajectories. My contribution is centered on these baseline experiments and their analysis, rather than ownership of the overall paper method.

sections.title: Reading the trade-off
sections.body: The comparison considers both adaptation to new trajectories and performance on the original sensing distribution. This makes the trade-off visible: an adaptation strategy needs to be assessed for what it gains under a new trajectory and what it may lose under the original one.

projects.evidenceStatus: Personal contribution: baseline comparisons; ICLR 2027 submission confirmed by the owner and the authored case study. Author position is not specified.

projects.title: Choosing what a model learns next
projects.subtitle: Learning to select useful examples—and learning when to rethink the selection strategy.
projects.summary: Can better training examples make a model learn more from less? From neural query policies to error-reduction sampling and training-batch completion.

sections.title: Learning a query policy
sections.body: I prototyped a neural-network / reinforcement-learning query strategy for continuous sample spaces, comparing its proposals with uniformly sampled candidates. Proposal rankings exposed instability, alongside data hunger and continual-learning limitations.

sections.title: Moving toward error reduction
sections.body: I developed self-supervised error-reduction sampling and compared it with random, uncertainty and diversity strategies. Archived figures cover an MLP toy problem and a Burgers’ equation experiment labeled FNO on the original website.

sections.title: Completing a training batch
sections.body: I explored error-reduction sampling as a complement to an existing batch-selection strategy, with coreset as the preferred base in that investigation. I considered sample efficiency, computational cost and the limits of the recorded results.

projects.dateNote: Original figures retain their experimental contexts: query policy, MLP toy problem, FNO-labeled Burgers run and training-only batch-completion comparison. The resume separately names DeepONet; the available sources do not establish how these records relate, so the archived FNO figure is not relabeled.

projects.title: Relativity you can interact with
projects.subtitle: Helping a guided VR lesson stay physically accurate—and assess what learners understand.
projects.summary: A narrative VR lesson on special relativity. I reviewed the physics and helped extend the learning assessment; the team evaluated the experience with 28 participants.

sections.title: A guided encounter with relativity
sections.body: The team developed a beginner-friendly, narrative VR lesson built around a train, a platform and an Albert guide. Learners compare reference frames, investigate length contraction and time dilation, and resolve a train-and-platform version of the barn paradox.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.body: I reviewed the physical correctness of the animations, verified relativistic parameters and helped adjust the Unity simulation. I also extended assessment questions to better probe conceptual understanding and the learning opportunities offered by VR, alongside literature review and instructional refinement.

sections.title: Team evaluation
sections.body: The extended abstract reports an evaluation with 28 participants using pre- and posttests and interviews, finding learning on several special-relativity concepts. These are team-level findings, without a claim of superiority over other teaching formats.

projects.dateNote: Period follows the existing resume. The user supplied the N=28 extended abstract, course design and assessment contribution on 2026-10-07. No publication venue, effect size or validated instrument name was supplied.

projects.title: Westlake iGEM 2024
projects.subtitle: Connecting biological questions, mathematical models, and a public-facing research wiki.
projects.role: Dry-lab group leader · Mathematical modeling & wiki development
projects.summary: I led the dry-lab group, developed mathematical models, and designed and built the wiki for Westlake’s 2024 iGEM project, alongside research writing and public engagement.

sections.title: A shared synthetic-biology project
sections.body: T-SAT explored engineered Salmonella as a delivery system for targeted cancer therapy. Our team combined biological design, laboratory experiments, mathematical modeling, and public engagement. My work connected the project’s quantitative questions with the website through which we explained our approach, methods, and findings.

sections.title: My role and contribution
sections.body: As dry-lab group leader, I coordinated the group’s work and project progress while contributing to conceptualization, literature review, experimental-data analysis, data curation, writing, and visualization. I was responsible for wiki design and development and for mathematical-model development. I also wrote research content for the wiki, particularly the model page, and contributed to public engagement.

sections.title: Developing the mathematical model
sections.body: I developed the mathematical-modeling work and documented its assumptions, equations, implementation, and interpretation. The framework follows three stages: bacterial transport from an injection point toward a tumor; bacterial growth, AHL signaling, and threshold-triggered lysis; and tumor-cell dynamics under the modeled Bax-mediated effect. It gave us a quantitative way to explore how the biological mechanisms relate to one another.

sections.title: From equations to numerical analysis
sections.body: For the bacterial-transport component, I worked through both circular-plane and spherical tumor geometries, accounting for movement, distance, and immune clearance. The Python implementation documented in the wiki uses NumPy, SymPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib for symbolic expressions, numerical integration, root finding, and visualization. The later components describe population growth and signaling through differential equations. The model page also discusses parameter choices and simplifications. The simulations explore the behavior of the proposed system under these stated assumptions.

sections.title: Designing and building the wiki
sections.body: I designed and developed the research wiki: its visual identity, page layouts, navigation, animated homepage, and presentation of scientific content. Built with Flask templates, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, it connects project descriptions, experimental work, mathematical models, team information, and human-practice activities. My role included implementing and editing pages as well as turning technical material into explanations and visualizations for visitors.

sections.title: Leading and communicating across disciplines
sections.body: I organized dry-lab activities, tracked progress, and coordinated project tasks with the team. Beyond coding and modeling, I contributed to science popularization, conversations with frontline doctors, and exchanges with other iGEM teams. These activities formed part of my human-practice and public-engagement work, alongside the literature research and writing that supported the project.
